newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Presidency meeting gathers old foes.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Presidency meeting gathers old foes.

text.p: If Bosnia's new three-man Presidency meets in Sarajevo on Monday for the first time as expected, three old foes -- Moslem, Serb and Croat -- will gather under the anxious eyes of the international community.
Their goal under the terms of the Dayton peace agreement is to stitch Bosnia back together again as a single, sovereign nation after Europe's worst war in half a century.
Sceptics predict the collective Presidency will become bogged down in the ethnic politics of which each member is a past master.
Certainly the Serb and Croat members pay lip service to Dayton while making no secret of their separatist desires.
The results of September 14 national balloting were certified on Sunday, clearing the way for formation of the new Bosnian government.
Alija Izetbegovic, who emerged top in the presidential elections, will serve as the Presidency's Chairman for the next two years.
He led Bosnian Moslems through 43-months of war, arguing the country should be preserved as a multi-ethnic haven.
Izetbegovic, an austere 70, cannot claim that his side triumphed. But it did survive, an outcome far from certain in the early days of the conflict.
A former political prisoner under Marshal Tito, he is suspected by many, including his Presidency colleagues, of harbouring fundamentalist Islamic tendencies.

The second-place finisher in presidency voting, by just 41,000 votes, was Momcilo Krajisnik, an unapologetic hardline separatist who has been at the heart of the Bosnian Serb leadership since war broke out in April 1992.

Krajisnik emerged from the shadow of former Serb President Radovan Karadzic and army commander General Ratko Mladic this year after the international community drove both men from public life as twice-indicted war criminals.
Tough and wily under an unbroken shelf of dark, bushy eyebrows, Krajisnik is now undisputed leader on the Serb side.
Kresimir Zubak, 49, the Croat member, is a war veteran who was wounded defending his native Doboj against Serb forces.
A judge before the war, he has become the public face for Bosnian Croat policies which most observers believe originate in Zagreb, the capital of neighbouring Croatia.

International mediator Carl Bildt has been working for months to smooth the way for the formation of the common governmental institutions envisioned under Dayton and has been a prime mover in arranging the first meeting of the Presidency.
"This is the first day for full implementation of the new constitution," Bildt spokesman Michael Maclay said on Monday.

"It's especially important in our view that they (the collective Presidency) should start the process of setting up a new council of ministers. The old government can only operate now on a purely administrative, caretaker basis."

Just arranging a first meeting of the Presidency has been a torturous process because of disputes over a time and place and security arrangements, not to mention the agenda. The next step will be to convene a meeting of the new national assembly.
